items.title: Tivaouane : mise en service progressive de l’hôpital Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy
items.description: Le ministre de la Santé et de l’Hygiène publique, Ibrahima Sy, et le ministre des Infrastructures, Déthié Fall, ont procédé à la mise en service progressive du Centre hospitalier national Seydi El Hadji Malick Sy, en présence d’une délégation du khalife général des Tidianes. Le ministre de la Santé précise qu’il s’agit d’une prise en main en deux phases. La première semaine sera consacrée à la formation des équipes. Les premières consultations débuteront durant la semaine du 17 août. L’inauguration officielle se fera en présence du président de la République. Ce démarrage progressif vise à garantir la maîtrise technique des équipements et la sécurité des patients. L’hôpital, de niveau 3, répond à la volonté de rapprocher les soins spécialisés des populations du Nord et des cités religieuses. Le ministre annonce également la construction d’une centaine de centres de santé et d’autres hôpitaux de niveau 3. Il indique que l’État s’oriente vers des « centres hospitaliers d’excellence », dotés notamment de services de radiothérapie et de transplantation. Le représentant du khalife, Serigne Habib Sy Mansour, a sollicité la création d’une unité de radiothérapie. Le ministre des Infrastructures a, pour sa part, appelé à accélérer les travaux afin de permettre une ouverture complète de l’établissement après le Gamou. Déthié Fall a invité l’entreprise et le FONSIS à lever toutes les contraintes afin d’achever les travaux de finition. Ibrahima NDIAYE Correspondant

items.title: 3rd phase of AJK elections: PML-N poised for gains in Poonch amid rigging allegations
items.description: The PML-N appeared set to gain at least one seat in Poonch division, where four constituencies went to the polls on Monday amid allegations of rigging, violence and disruption, with polling suspended at some places. The biggest upset was the defeat of Muslim Conference president Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan in LA-14 (Dhirkot), a constituency from where he, and before him his uncle and father, had been elected in all nine elections since 1985. His defeat also appeared to underscore the political decline of what was once the largest and longest-ruling party in Azad Jammu and Kashmir (AJK), but was reduced to a marginal force following the emergence of the PML-N in 2010. Khan was defeated by Sajid Iqbal Abbasi, who contested his first election on the ticket of the little-known Awami Dast-o-Bazu Party, by a margin of more than 21,000 votes, according to unofficial and unverified results from 213 of the 214 polling stations. Observers attributed Abbasi’s victory largely to his hands-on efforts for the development of the constituency and the welfare of its residents, which, they said, had helped him build a personal support base over the years. PML-N’s Raja Faisal Azad and PPP’s Raja Mubashar Ejaz secured 3,000 and 2,800 votes, respectively. In another closely watched contest in LA-17 (Haveli), a neck-and-neck fight was under way between Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore and PML-N candidate Engr Chaudhry Mohsin Aziz. Initial reports suggested that Aziz had established a sizeable lead, but it later emerged that results from nearly two dozen polling stations were still awaited. Independent candidate Khawaja Tariq Saeed, who had initially been tipped to finish second, was trailing far behind. In LA-15 (Bagh Central), Jamaat-i-Islami’s Brig (retd) Dr Mohammad Khan was initially reported to be heading for victory, but the contest later narrowed to a two-way race between PML-N’s Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas and PPP’s Sardar Ziaul Qamar. Late-night unofficial and unverified results showed Qamar establishing a clear lead of 2,000 votes over Mr Minhas. Istehkam-i-Pakistan Party (IPP) president and former AJK prime minister Sardar Tanveer Ilyas, who had won the constituency in the 2021 election on a PTI ticket, appeared to be out of the race. In LA-16 (Bagh East), PML-N’s Sardar Mir Akbar was leading PPP’s Sardar Qamaruz Zaman, who is the father of the PPP candidate in LA-15 and has served as an AJK minister in several PPP governments. Akbar had secured 14,900 votes, while Mr Qamar had polled 10,960. Results from 14 polling stations were awaited. Elections are being held across AJK in phases amid tensions between protesters and the authorities. Citing law and order concerns, the Election Commission had decided to postpone polling in Bagh and Sudhnoti districts that was originally set for today. Polling began at 8am and continued until 5pm in four Poonch constituencies. The PPP, which has accused the PML-N of rigging in the previous phases, continued to make similar allegations on Monday as well. In response, PML-N leaders said the PPP had no evidence for its claims, and reiterated their confidence to form the government in AJK based on the seats it has already secured so far. The PML-N has so far bagged 24 seats — nine from Mirpur polls held on July 27 and 15 in the second phase comprising Muzaffarabad Division and the 12 refugee seats. On the other hand, the PPP has only won 10 constituencies so far. The third phase of the AJK elections was originally meant to cover all of Poonch Division. The division comprises 11 constituencies, including three in Bagh, one in Haveli, five in Poonch district and two in Sudhnoti district. However, last week the AJK Election Commission announced that polling would only go ahead as scheduled in Bagh and Haveli due to concerns over the law and order situation. The AJK election commissioner has hinted that polling on the remaining seven constituencies could be held by Aug 20 or 21. Government officials had anticipated clashes in some areas today, while the Election Commission had classified most of the 803 polling stations in the four constituencies as either sensitive or highly sensitive. “Apart from the regular police of both districts, we have dispatched an additional 10,300 troops to maintain law and order and provide a fear-free atmosphere to voters,” Election Commission Secretary Raja Mohammad Shakeel told Dawn earlier Malpractice, rigging allegations Polling in previous phases of the elections was marred by allegations of rigging , scuffles and violence, with the PPP and the PML-N — the main contenders in AJK but allies in the Centre — engaging in a war of words. The PPP has accused the PML-N of rigging and electoral malpractices in the previous phases. It continued to allege rigging in Haveli and Bagh as well. In a series of posts on X, the PPP shared complaints it said it had filed to the Election Commission. In one of the complaints, the PPP alleged that roads leading to the Banni Marasira area had been blocked, where PML-N supporters were illegally stamping ballot papers at 12 polling stations in the LA-15 constituency. “The commission is requested to consider the two acts together rather than separately, because the second is made possible by the first,” the party said, adding that officials, voters, polling agents and party workers were unable to reach the polling stations “to see what is being done inside”. The party also claimed delays in polling at LA-15’s polling station no.87 in Thub. It also alleged that polling at stations no.143 and 144 in Hatala Pader did not commence on time due to the non-arrival of polling staff. The PPP also alleged that its polling agent was “forcibly removed” from LA-15’s station no.158 in Makhdoom Kot. Similarly, PPP’s agents had also been removed from polling stations no.8-14 in Bani Maldhara and PML-N supporters were stamping ballot papers at those stations, the party alleged. At around 12:45, the party claimed on X that workers of Jamaat-i-Islami had gathered to “capture” 26 polling stations in the constituency — nos.31-38, nos.70-79 and nos.180-186. It said the police had initially arrived but then withdrew. “The stations are, therefore, unguarded at this moment, with an organised body assembled against them.” It urged the Election Commission to determine on whose orders police had withdrawn and direct the law enforcers to return to the station. The PPP also posted a blurry video, which it said was of PML-N workers “attacking” the polling station set up at the Boys Middle School in LA-15 Central Bagh. Regarding LA-16, the party claimed that its polling agents were not being allowed inside stations no.119 and 120 while PML-N supporters were stamping ballot papers inside the stations in the agents’ absence. The PPP further alleged delays in polling at stations no.61 and 141 of the constituency. It made similar allegations regarding polling stations no.109 and 110 in LA-16 Bagh-III Sharqi. Moreover, the party accused “armed individuals associated with the PML-N” of opening fire at polling station no.179, Kot Chinalla in the constituency and disrupting the election process. “The polling agents of the PPP have been removed from the station. It is further alleged that ballot papers are being stamped lawfully,” the PPP added. In LA-17, the party alleged that its agents had been “forced out” from the polling station in Mullah Basti, Kahuta City by PML-N workers. PPP Vice President Sherry Rehman expressed reservations after reports of rigging and malpractices emerged, saying that preventing polling agents from entering polling stations in LA-16 raised “serious questions” about the transparency of the election process. In a statement, she demanded that an explanation be sought from the presiding officers of stations nos.119 and 120 on the matter. The senator also called for the Election Commission to take notice of the reports of PPP’s polling agent being removed from station no.158 in LA-15. Rehman further demanded alternative arrangements to compensate for the shortage of polling staff and material, calling on the authorities to ensure that free and transparent elections were held at all polling stations without any disruption. PPP Secretary General Nayyar Bokhari also accused the PML-N of continuing rigging in the third phase of the elections. He highlighted that his party was regularly informing the Election Commission about the alleged rigging via phone. But, “the chief election commissioner and the election commission secretary’s reply to all of our complaints has been that nothing has happened and everything is good,” he claimed. When Dawn approached the Election Commission regarding Bokhari’s claim, Secretary Raja Muhammad Shakeel said any complaint that he or the chief election commissioner received was being attended and responded to, and the Quick Response Force (QRF) was also moved over it. ‘AJK’s people have supported PML-N’ Responding to PPP’s allegations, Adviser to the Prime Minister on Political Affairs Rana Sanaullah said the rival party had not provided any proof for its claims. Addressing a press conference in Islamabad flanked by Minister for Kashmir Affairs Amir Muqam, Sanaullah denied that a comparatively high turnout could be considered proof of rigging. The PML-N leader explained that a strong family and tribe system in AJK prompted people to show up for their relatives. “Our opposing candidate Chaudhry Yasin was complaining yesterday that in his opposing candidate’s union council (UC), 80pc votes were cast, whereas in his own UC, 96pc votes were cast,” Sanaullah claimed. Sanaullah asserted that balloting had gone fairly smoothly in Bagh and Haveli today. He, however, detailed a few reported incidents. In Haveli, people tried to snatch documents from the polling agents in one station, but the Quick Response Force (QRF) promptly responded and resolved the situation without incident, according to Sanaullah. In Bagh, some people, whom Sanaullah claimed were PPP workers, tried to halt polling at three stations. QRF responded there as well and resumed polling, the minister added. Meanwhile, Muqam urged PPP to review the number of people attending their rallies instead of accusing others of rigging, insisting that PPP lacked support from the people of AJK. “AJK’s people have supported PML-N,” Muqam asserted. Disputing PPP’s recent stance that it was against phased elections, Muqam said the party had mentioned no reservations when the election schedule was first announced . Sanaullah also backed Muqam, saying that PPP had not raised concerns when the Election Commission had originally sought consent from all parties for phased elections. He further claimed that upon PPP’s insistence, the electoral watchdog had scheduled voting on the 12 refugee seats in the second phase of the elections. Sanaullah contended that PPP did not want election results from the refugee seats in the rest of Pakistan to impact its numbers in AJK polls since PPP had not even canvassed in those places. Speaking about the recent unrest in the region, Sanaullah expressed hope that the protests would end once the third phase of elections concludes, as protesters had “only aimed to stop elections”. The new AJK government, which he said PML-N would form with a two-thirds majority, will respond to the protesters’ “valid demands”, the PML-N leader added. However, he also warned that those who “took up arms and instigated the people of AJK, while acting on the directions of the enemy… will have to face the law and answer for their crimes”. In response to a reporter’s question about PPP’s claim that PML-N only had numbered days of rule in the Centre, Sanaullah expressed hope that after the AJK elections, PPP would “open-heartedly” congratulate PML-N. Meanwhile, PML-N’s AJK chapter secretary general Tariq Farooq — who also emerged as the winner in LA-7 recently — said allegations of “rigging, violence, coercion, or fake voting” emerging from the constituency of Prime Minister Faisal Mumtaz Rathore were a “serious question of constitutional governance”. “This is no longer merely an electoral dispute. It becomes a serious question of constitutional governance, democratic values, and the sanctity of the people’s vote,” Farooq wrote on X. “I find it difficult to believe that the prime minister of Azad Jammu & Kashmir could consider himself above the Constitution, the law, and basic ethical obligations merely to secure his own election,” he said, without providing further details. The PML-N candidate asserted that “public mandate must be secured through a free, fair and transparent election, not through power, influence or state authority”. Rathore, two ex-AJK PMs face crucial electoral test In Monday’s polls, AJK PM Rathore, who is from the PPP, and two of his predecessors — Sardar Tanveer Ilyas and Sardar Attique Ahmed Khan — face a battle for political survival as voters head to the polls. Around 238,664 men and 221,707 women are eligible to cast their ballots at 803 polling stations comprising 1,254 polling booths. A total of 82 candidates are in the fray, with LA-14 (Dhirkot) attracting the highest number of candidates at 30 and LA-17 (Haveli) the lowest at nine. In LA-17, Rathore is facing PML-N candidate Mohsin Aziz and independent candidate Khawaja Tariq Saeed, a member of the AJK Council. Rathore and Saeed had been political allies and, under an agreement, had agreed to contest the seat alternately. However, after becoming prime minister, Rathore asked Saeed to step aside in his favour, a request he did not accept, turning the former allies into rivals. Aziz, whose father Chaudhry Mohammad Aziz had won the seat at least three times, draws support from the sizeable Gujjar community. His recent large election rally in Forward Kahuta reportedly surprised his rivals and underscored the strength of his campaign. Saeed, meanwhile, is believed to enjoy the backing of a sizeable section of the Kashmiri community, as well as an alliance of several smaller clans. Rathore, however, remains confident of retaining the seat, citing the performance of his government during his relatively brief tenure as prime minister. The constituency has also witnessed allegations of electoral irregularities on social media, with reports claiming that two presiding officers had been caught manipulating results in favour of Rathore. Shakeel dismissed the allegations but at the same time confirmed that complaints had been received against the two officials and that they had subsequently been relieved of election duties. In LA-15 (Wasti Bagh), ex-PM Ilyas is facing PML-N candidate and former minister Mushtaq Ahmed Minhas, PPP nominee and sitting minister Sardar Ziaul Qamar, and Jamaat-i-Islami candidate retired Brig Dr Mohammad Khan, a respected educationist. Ilyas, who secured a little over 3,300 votes from Upper Neelum in the second phase of the elections, had initially announced a boycott of the third phase. He subsequently reversed the decision and resumed campaigning, claiming that his victory would enable the constituency to “secure either the presidency or prime ministership.” Ilyas and Qamar belong to the same Madiyal tribe, while Brig Khan belongs to the Narma clan and enjoys the support of former JI chief Abdul Rashid Turabi and former adviser Raja Yasin Khan. Minhas has the advantage of belonging to the PML-N, which is poised to form the next government after emerging as the largest party in the elections held so far. His campaign has also stressed the argument that voters should elect a candidate from the party that is set to occupy the government benches rather than send their representative to the opposition. In LA-16 (Sharqi Bagh), former ministers Sardar Mir Akbar and Sardar Qamar Zaman are the principal contenders, representing the PML-N and PPP, respectively. The fourth contest, LA-14 (Dhirkot), has drawn particular attention because of the challenge faced by Sardar Attique, head of the once-dominant Muslim Conference (MC). Attique is reportedly facing a strong challenge from Sajid Iqbal Abbasi of the relatively new Awam Dast-o-Bazu Party. A contractor and philanthropist, Abbasi is said to have spent millions of rupees from his own resources on public welfare projects in the constituency, helping him build a sizeable personal following. Attique, who has represented the constituency successively since 2006, when he first became prime minister, faces an additional challenge in that Abbasi also belongs to the same tribe. Among nearly two dozen other candidates are PML-N’s nominee Raja Faisal Azad and PPP candidate Raja Mubashar Ejaz. While the main contest is seen as being between Attique and Abbasi, the PML-N and PPP nominees are expected to vie for the second runner-up position. Additional reporting by Tariq Naqash

items.title: No Roof, no future: Ghana’s rent crisis is turning survival into a luxury
items.description: Imagine working for an entire month and, before you have even received your salary, knowing that a large part of it already belongs to your landlord. Imagine spending years in school, earning a qualification, finally securing a job and discovering that independence comes with a price you cannot afford. Imagine being a parent forced to choose between paying rent, buying food for your children and paying their school expenses. For many Ghanaians, these are not imaginary situations. They are everyday realities. The search for accommodation in Ghana has become more than a search for a place to sleep. For an increasing number of people, it is a struggle for dignity, stability and the right to build a normal life. The question is no longer simply, “Where can I find a room?” It is, “How much of my life must I sacrifice to afford one?” That is the painful reality of Ghana’s housing and rent crisis. Across the country, particularly in rapidly growing urban and educational communities, the cost of accommodation continues to place enormous pressure on households. As populations increase and people move towards areas where jobs, schools and businesses are concentrated, the demand for housing continues to rise. But for the ordinary Ghanaian, income has not necessarily risen at the same pace. The result is a painful imbalance: expensive accommodation on one side and limited incomes on the other. And somewhere in the middle is the Ghanaian trying desperately to survive. A young graduate may spend years listening to parents say, “Just finish school and get a job. Things will become better.” Then graduation comes. The certificate is framed. The job application is submitted. Eventually, employment arrives. But instead of the freedom that was imagined, another problem appears. Rent. The young worker begins searching for a room and discovers that securing one requires money that could take months or even years to accumulate. If the room is affordable, it may be far from work. If it is close to work, it may be too expensive. The choice becomes painful: live far away and spend heavily on transportation, or live closer and surrender a significant portion of the salary to rent. For some young people, this is where the dream of independence begins to collapse. They return to their parents’ homes. Not because they are lazy. Not because they do not want to become independent. But because the mathematics simply does not work. This is one of the quiet frustrations of being young in Ghana today. Young people are told to work hard, acquire skills, become independent and build their future. But what happens when the first step toward independence—a decent place to live—is financially out of reach? The advance-rent burden Then there is the issue of advance rent. For many tenants, paying monthly rent is difficult enough. Having to produce a large amount of money upfront makes the situation even more challenging. A person may have a monthly income but still be unable to secure accommodation because their savings cannot cover the required advance payment. This creates a cruel situation. You can have a job and still struggle to find a home. You can earn a salary and still be unable to move out of your parents’ house. You can work every day and still remain financially trapped. Some people borrow from relatives. Some take loans. Others spend their entire savings. By the time they finally get the keys to the room, they may already be carrying a financial burden that follows them for years. A home is supposed to provide security. But for many tenants, the journey into a home begins with debt. Students are not spared The accommodation crisis is equally painful for students. For a student who has travelled from another region to attend university, gaining admission should be a moment of celebration. Parents should be thinking about tuition, books and academic needs. Instead, accommodation can become one of the first and most frightening financial challenges. Rooms close to campuses can be expensive. Affordable options may be located far away. Some students share rooms with several people simply because that is what their families can afford. Others spend hours travelling to lectures. And every day spent travelling is another day in which time, energy and money are lost. A student who should be preparing for an examination may instead be worrying about where to sleep next semester. A parent who has struggled to pay school fees may suddenly be confronted with another demand for accommodation. Education is supposed to create opportunities and break cycles of poverty. It should not create a new cycle of accommodation insecurity. When cheaper accommodation comes with another price But even finding cheaper accommodation does not necessarily mean the problem is solved. Sometimes the cheaper room comes with poor sanitation, unreliable water, inadequate ventilation, overcrowding, leaking roofs or unsafe surroundings. For families with children, the consequences can be particularly serious. Imagine raising children in a room where several people share limited space, where proper ventilation is lacking and where basic sanitation is inadequate. Imagine a child trying to study in a crowded room because the family cannot afford anything better. We must ask ourselves: At what point does affordable housing become too expensive if the price is human dignity? Being poor should not mean being forced to live in unsafe conditions. Rent is eating more than salaries The cost of accommodation also affects what happens outside the home. When people cannot afford to live close to their workplaces, they move farther away. Then comes transportation. The worker wakes up before dawn, joins an overcrowded vehicle, spends hours on the road and arrives at work already exhausted. At the end of the day, the journey begins again. The money saved on rent may then disappear into transportation costs. This creates a vicious cycle. Cheap accommodation can mean expensive transportation. Expensive accommodation can mean financial hardship. And somewhere between the two, the ordinary worker is struggling to breathe. The cost is not only financial. It is emotional. It is the stress of constantly calculating whether the salary will last. It is the fear of receiving a notice that the rent is due. It is the embarrassment of repeatedly asking family members for help. It is the frustration of working hard and still feeling as though one is standing in the same place. It is the exhaustion of spending hours commuting because home is too expensive and work is too far away. These are the hidden costs of Ghana’s housing crisis. The family is also paying the price Housing insecurity does not affect individuals alone. It affects families. A young couple may postpone marriage because they cannot afford accommodation. Parents may delay having another child because they are struggling to provide adequate space for the children they already have. Families may remain in overcrowded houses because moving into a better apartment would consume too much of their income. Some young adults remain dependent on their parents well into adulthood because the cost of independent living is simply too high. The housing crisis is therefore influencing personal decisions that should ideally be based on choice rather than financial desperation. And this should concern us as a nation. What kind of development are we building? Ghana often speaks about development in terms of roads, buildings, economic growth, investment and urban expansion. But development must ultimately be about people. What does economic growth mean to the worker who cannot afford rent? What does urban development mean to the family living in an overcrowded room? What does employment mean to the graduate whose entire income disappears into accommodation and transportation? What does progress mean to the student who cannot find a safe place to live? These questions deserve honest answers. A country cannot call itself successful simply because it is building more houses. The important question is: Who can afford to live in them? If the average worker cannot afford the homes being constructed, then the country is building houses without solving the housing problem. Government cannot look away Government has a major responsibility in addressing this crisis. Affordable housing must become a long-term national priority rather than a political slogan that appears during election campaigns and disappears afterwards. Ghana needs stronger partnerships between the public and private sectors to increase the supply of genuinely affordable homes. Housing finance must become more accessible. Land administration must improve. Urban planning must be strengthened. Local authorities must ensure that expanding communities have adequate roads, drainage, water, sanitation, electricity, schools and healthcare facilities. And tenancy laws must be properly enforced. Tenants also need greater awareness of their rights and responsibilities. Landlords have legitimate costs and responsibilities, and not every landlord is responsible for the housing crisis. But where exploitative practices occur, tenants must have effective avenues for protection and redress. The solution must be balanced, practical and long-term. A house is not just a building Perhaps the biggest mistake we make when discussing housing is treating it as merely a construction issue. A house is where a child does homework. It is where a mother prepares food after a long day at work. It is where a father rests after spending hours earning a living. It is where students prepare for examinations. It is where couples build families. It is where people recover from the pressures of the outside world. A home provides psychological and emotional security. When that security becomes uncertain, the effects can reach every aspect of life. That is why the rent crisis should not be treated as a private inconvenience. It is a national development issue. The market woman deserves a safe home. The teacher deserves a decent home. The nurse deserves a decent home. The driver deserves a decent home. The farmer deserves a decent home. The graduate deserves a decent home. The student deserves a safe place to study and sleep. The ordinary Ghanaian deserves more than simply surviving from one rent deadline to another. Ghana must act before the crisis becomes normal The greatest danger is that we may become accustomed to the crisis. We may begin to believe that expensive rent is simply part of life. We may accept overcrowding as normal. We may accept young adults remaining permanently dependent on their parents. We may accept workers spending hours commuting every day. We may accept families sacrificing food and education to pay rent. We may accept the idea that owning or even comfortably renting a home is only for the wealthy. We must not. A decent home should not be a privilege reserved for people with high incomes or powerful connections. Housing is fundamental to human dignity. If Ghana wants productive workers, we need stable homes. If Ghana wants successful students, we need safe accommodation. If Ghana wants strong families, we need affordable housing. If Ghana wants young people to build their future here, we must make it possible for them to actually live here with dignity. The housing crisis is therefore not simply about landlords and tenants. It is about the kind of country we want to become. Do we want a country where people work simply to pay rent? Do we want a country where young people postpone their dreams because they cannot afford a room? Do we want a country where families remain trapped in overcrowded homes because decent accommodation is beyond their reach? Or do we want a Ghana where working hard provides a genuine path to stability? The answer should be obvious. No roof, no stability. No stability, no meaningful progress. Ghana cannot continue to demand productivity from people whose basic living conditions remain insecure. We must build more affordable homes, strengthen the rental system, enforce existing protections and plan our cities around the people who actually live and work in them. Because at the heart of this crisis is a simple truth: The Ghanaian is not asking for a mansion. They are asking for somewhere safe to call home. And in a country blessed with human resources, land and enormous potential, that should never be too much to ask.

items.title: Domestic violence in Ghana: The crisis behind close doors
items.description: Home is supposed to be the place where fear ends. It is where a person should be able to close the door behind them, breathe freely and know that they are safe. It is where children should learn what love looks like, where couples should find companionship, and where families should find comfort after the pressures of the outside world. But for too many people in Ghana, closing the door does not bring safety. It brings fear. Behind the walls of ordinary homes, some people are living with threats, insults, intimidation, beatings, sexual abuse, financial control and psychological torment. Some wake up every morning wondering what will trigger the next outburst. Others have become so accustomed to abuse that they have stopped recognising their own suffering as something that deserves attention. From the outside, everything may look normal. A family may attend church together. They may appear together at social gatherings. They may post smiling photographs online. Neighbours may describe them as a “good family.” Yet behind the door, someone may be crying. This is the uncomfortable reality of domestic violence in Ghana. It is a crisis that does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it hides behind makeup, long sleeves, excuses, silence and carefully constructed smiles. And because much of it happens away from public view, society can underestimate its scale and seriousness. Domestic violence must therefore be understood as more than physical assault. It can take the form of emotional and psychological abuse, sexual violence, economic abuse, threats, intimidation, stalking, humiliation, isolation, controlling behaviour and destruction of property. A person does not have to walk into a hospital with a broken bone before society takes their suffering seriously. A woman who is constantly told that she is useless is being harmed. A man whose movements, friendships and finances are controlled through threats is being harmed. A child who watches one parent violently abuse another is being harmed. An elderly relative who is threatened, neglected or financially exploited within a household is being harmed. The wounds may not always be visible, but the damage is real. The first challenge Ghana must confront is the culture of silence surrounding domestic violence. For generations, many families have been taught to protect the reputation of the household at almost any cost. When a woman reports that her husband is abusing her, relatives may tell her to be patient. When a husband reports abuse, he may be laughed at. When a young person complains about violence at home, they may be told not to expose family matters. When neighbours hear repeated arguments, they may decide that it is not their business. When religious leaders become involved, the emphasis may sometimes be placed so heavily on preserving the relationship that the safety of the victim becomes secondary. This must change. There is nothing honourable about protecting the reputation of a family while a member of that family is being destroyed. There is no peace in a home where one person is afraid of another. And there is no strength in a family that survives by forcing its most vulnerable member to suffer in silence. The phrase “it is a family matter” must no longer be used as an excuse to look away. Domestic violence becomes a national issue the moment it threatens the safety, health and dignity of citizens. It becomes a national issue when children are traumatised. It becomes a national issue when victims require medical care. It becomes a national issue when workers lose productivity because of physical and psychological injuries. It becomes a national issue when families are destroyed. And it becomes an even greater national tragedy when violence ends in death. The country cannot wait for the worst possible outcome before taking the problem seriously. Another reason victims remain trapped is economic dependence. For a person who has no stable income, leaving an abusive home can appear almost impossible. A mother may know that her partner is dangerous, but she may also know that she cannot immediately afford rent. She may wonder where her children will sleep. She may worry about school fees. She may fear losing access to food, healthcare and other basic necessities. A victim may therefore remain in a dangerous relationship not because they approve of the abuse, but because they are calculating the consequences of leaving. This is why economic empowerment must be part of the domestic violence conversation. Skills training, employment opportunities, access to financial services, safe accommodation and social support can give victims options. A person should never have to choose between physical safety and economic survival. But financial dependence is not the only chain. Fear is another. Some victims have been threatened with death. Some are told that their children will be taken away. Some are threatened with public shame. Some are warned that their families will be attacked. Others have been abused for so long that their confidence has been systematically destroyed. An abuser may repeatedly tell a victim that nobody else will love them. They may say that the victim is worthless. They may convince the victim that the abuse is their fault. Over time, the victim may begin to believe it. This is why psychological abuse deserves the same seriousness as physical violence. A wound on the body may heal. The belief that you are worthless can remain for years. Children also carry a heavy burden in homes where violence occurs. A child does not need to be directly beaten to become a victim of domestic violence. Hearing threats, witnessing assaults and living in an atmosphere of fear can profoundly affect a child’s emotional and psychological development. A child who should be thinking about school may instead be listening for the sound of an angry parent approaching. A child who should be sleeping peacefully may be wondering whether another argument will begin during the night. Some children become withdrawn. Some become aggressive. Some struggle academically. Some develop anxiety. Others may grow up believing that violence is simply part of family life. This is where the crisis becomes generational. Children learn what relationships look like by observing adults. If violence is repeatedly presented as normal, some may eventually reproduce the same behaviour in their own relationships. The cycle continues. That is why breaking domestic violence is not only about protecting today’s victims. It is about protecting tomorrow’s generation. Ghana must also be careful not to reduce the conversation to women alone. Women and girls face significant risks of domestic and gender-based violence, and their protection must remain a priority. However, men can also experience abuse, and male victims often face a different kind of silence. A man who reports that his partner is physically or emotionally abusing him may be mocked. He may be told to defend himself. He may be accused of being weak. He may fear that nobody will believe him. This culture of ridicule can prevent male victims from seeking help. The message must be clear: violence is wrong regardless of who commits it and regardless of who suffers it. Protecting victims should never become a gender competition. The goal is safety, justice and prevention. There is also a group that is frequently forgotten in conversations about domestic violence: older people. Elderly parents and relatives can experience neglect, intimidation, physical abuse and financial exploitation from people within their own households. Some are too dependent on their caregivers to report what is happening. Some fear being abandoned. Others remain silent because they do not want to see their own children punished. Their vulnerability makes their protection particularly important. A society that values family must also protect those who become dependent on family members in old age. The legal framework is another important part of the conversation. Ghana has the Domestic Violence Act, 2007 (Act 732), which provides a legal framework for addressing domestic violence. But laws are meaningful only when victims can actually access protection and justice. A victim should not have to navigate a confusing system alone. Police officers, healthcare workers, social workers, lawyers and other professionals involved in domestic violence cases need appropriate training and resources. Reporting mechanisms must be accessible. Victims must be treated with dignity. Cases must be handled seriously. And where protection orders or other legal remedies are available, they must be meaningful in practice. The fear that “nothing will happen” can be enough to prevent a victim from reporting abuse. That fear must be defeated by a justice system that people can trust. However, the responsibility does not end with the police or courts. Healthcare facilities are often among the first places where victims appear. A person may arrive with injuries without openly saying what happened. Healthcare workers must therefore be equipped to recognise possible signs of abuse and respond sensitively. Social workers and support organisations also need adequate resources to help survivors rebuild their lives. It is not enough to help someone leave an abusive environment. We must ask what happens afterwards. Where will the survivor live? How will they earn an income? How will they care for their children? How will they recover psychologically? How will they rebuild their confidence? Leaving may be the beginning of the journey, not the end. Religious and traditional leaders also have enormous influence. Many Ghanaians turn to churches, mosques, traditional authorities and family elders during moments of crisis. This influence can be used positively. Leaders can educate their communities about healthy relationships, challenge harmful beliefs and encourage victims to seek appropriate help. But one message must be made clear: reconciliation should never come before safety. Telling an abused person to return to the same environment without addressing the danger is not necessarily reconciliation. Sometimes the most responsible intervention is to create distance, protect the victim and ensure that professional assistance is available. Marriage preservation must never become more important than human life. The media, too, must do more. Domestic violence stories often attract public attention when they involve severe injuries or death. But reporting should not begin only when tragedy occurs. Journalists should examine patterns. What happened before the violence escalated? Did the victim seek help? Were there previous complaints? Did relatives know? Were warning signs ignored? Were there institutional failures? What could have prevented the situation from becoming fatal? These are the questions that can turn reporting into public service. The media must also avoid victim-blaming. Instead of asking, “Why did she stay?”, society should ask why the perpetrator believed violence was acceptable. Instead of asking why a victim did not report earlier, we should ask whether the environment made reporting safe and accessible. Instead of turning survivors into objects of pity, we should give them dignity. Social media has created another dimension to the problem. Online platforms can help expose abuse and give victims a voice, but they can also encourage public shaming, misinformation and the circulation of sensitive images. A serious domestic violence case should not become entertainment for social media users. Behind every viral video may be a traumatised human being. Ghanaians must learn to respond with compassion rather than curiosity. Prevention must also begin before relationships become violent. Schools can play an important role by teaching children about respect, boundaries, emotional intelligence and healthy relationships. Young people need to understand that jealousy is not love. Possessiveness is not love. Control is not love. Threats are not love. And violence is certainly not love. Boys should be taught that masculinity does not require domination. Girls should be taught that they do not owe anyone their silence. Young people of all genders should learn that disagreement can exist without abuse. Families must also create environments where children feel safe enough to speak when something is wrong. The fight against domestic violence must become preventive rather than reactive. We cannot continue waiting until someone is seriously injured before we become concerned. We cannot wait until a child is traumatised before we ask questions. We cannot wait until another life is lost before the nation expresses outrage. Every violent incident that is ignored sends a message. Every victim who is dismissed sends a message. Every perpetrator who escapes accountability sends a message. And that message can encourage the next act of violence. Domestic violence also has economic consequences that deserve greater attention. When victims are injured, they may be unable to work. When children are traumatised, their education can suffer. When families break down, financial pressures increase. Healthcare costs rise. Legal processes consume resources. Productivity is lost. The consequences therefore extend far beyond the walls of the home. Domestic violence weakens families, communities and, ultimately, national development. A country cannot build a productive population while allowing large numbers of people to live in environments of fear and abuse. The fight against domestic violence therefore belongs in Ghana’s national development conversation. It belongs in discussions about healthcare. It belongs in education. It belongs in economic empowerment. It belongs in justice. It belongs in social protection. It belongs in community development. And it belongs in the national conversation about human rights and dignity. Ghana needs a coordinated response. Government agencies must work together. Law enforcement must be strengthened. Support services must be accessible. Shelters and safe spaces must be adequately supported. Public education must move beyond occasional campaigns. Schools must teach healthy relationships. Employers should understand how domestic violence can affect workers. Communities must stop protecting perpetrators through silence. Families must learn to support victims rather than shame them. Religious and traditional leaders must prioritise safety. And citizens must learn that noticing abuse and doing nothing is not neutrality. At the same time, prevention must include rehabilitation and behaviour-change programmes for perpetrators where appropriate. Punishment is necessary where the law requires it, but Ghana must also confront the beliefs and behaviours that produce violence. If a person leaves one abusive relationship and repeats the same behaviour with another partner, society has not solved the underlying problem. We need accountability, but we also need prevention. Ultimately, the question Ghana must answer is simple: What kind of society do we want to become? A society where families protect their image while victims suffer? A society where children grow up believing violence is normal? A society where victims are blamed for the actions of their abusers? Or a society where safety, dignity and respect are considered non-negotiable? The answer should not be difficult. Home must be safe. Marriage must be safe. Childhood must be safe. Old age must be safe. Relationships must be built on respect rather than fear. We must stop calling control love. We must stop calling violence discipline. We must stop calling silence peace. And we must stop treating domestic violence as a private matter that outsiders should never discuss. Because the truth is that there is nothing private about a national crisis that destroys lives, traumatises children, weakens families and places pressure on the country’s health, justice and social systems. Behind every statistic is a person. Behind every police report is a story. Behind every injury is pain. Behind every silent victim is a voice that may be waiting for someone to say, “You do not deserve this.” Ghana cannot afford to wait for another tragedy before acting. We must make it easier for victims to speak, safer for them to leave, harder for perpetrators to escape accountability and less acceptable for communities to look away. The battle against domestic violence will not be won by government alone. It will be won when parents teach their children respect, when communities refuse to protect abusers, when institutions respond with seriousness, when the media reports responsibly, when victims are supported rather than blamed, and when every Ghanaian understands that violence has no place in a healthy home. A home should be the first place where a child learns love. It should be the first place where an adult experiences security. It should be the place where people can remove their fears, not where new fears are created. Home should not be where violence begins. Home should be where safety begins. And until every Ghanaian can say that with confidence, the work of confronting domestic violence is far from over.

items.title: Prévention contre la rage | Les campagnes de vaccination gratuite se poursuivent
items.description: Dans le cadre de la poursuite des efforts de lutte contre la rage, les campagne de vaccination gratuite pour chiens et chats se poursuivent en Tunisie. En effet, les services vétérinaires relevant de la Commissariat régional au développement agricole (CRDA) de Nabeul ont organisé une vaste campagne de vaccination gratuiteà la place El Fehri, dans la délégation de Dar Chaâbane El Fehri. Cette initiative s'inscrit dans une démarche de proximité visant à rapprocher les services vétérinaires des citoyens et à faciliter l'accès au vaccin antirabique, indique la Direction générale des services vétérinaires. Les campagnes sont menées dans les espaces publics fréquentés pour permettre au plus grand nombre de propriétaires d'animaux de compagnie de bénéficier gratuitement de cette prestation essentielle. Au-delà de l'acte vaccinal, ces journées de terrain mettent l'accent sur la sensibilisation de la population face aux dangers de la rage et sur le rôle primordial des citoyens dans la chaîne de préventionn, ajoute la même source en rappelant l'importance d'une vaccination régulière des animaux domestiques, de la lutte contre l'errance canine non surveillée, ainsi que de la nécessité de signaler tout animal suspect ou de se rendre immédiatement dans un centre de santé en cas de morsure ou de griffure. items.title: Managem franchit un seuil historique de 11,8 milliards de dirhams de chiffre d'affaires
items.description: Le groupe minier marocain Managem a enregistré, au premier semestre 2026, les meilleurs résultats semestriels de son histoire. Porté par la montée en puissance de ses nouveaux projets miniers et par un environnement favorable sur les marchés des métaux, le groupe a réalisé un chiffre d'affaires consolidé de 11,764 milliards de dirhams, contre 4,4 milliards de dirhams un an auparavant, soit une progression de 166 % en glissement annuel. Cette performance marque un tournant pour le groupe, qui dépasse pour la première fois le seuil des 11 milliards de dirhams de revenus sur les six premiers mois d'un exercice. Dans sa communication financière, Managem attribue cette croissance à la contribution de ses nouveaux actifs stratégiques, tout en soulignant la résilience de ses activités historiques. Au cœur de cette dynamique figurent les mines de Tizert, dédiée à la production de cuivre au Maroc, et de Boto, spécialisée dans l'or au Sénégal. Les deux sites ont atteint leur capacité nominale de production, permettant au groupe de bénéficier pleinement d'un contexte de marché marqué par la hausse des cours des métaux. Cette évolution s'est accompagnée du maintien des bonnes performances des actifs historiques, renforçant ainsi la progression de l'activité. Le deuxième trimestre confirme cette accélération. Entre avril et juin 2026, Managem a réalisé un chiffre d'affaires légèrement supérieur à 6 milliards de dirhams, contre près de 2 milliards de dirhams à la même période de l'année précédente. Le groupe précise également que ce niveau représente une hausse de 4,5 % par rapport au trimestre précédent, traduisant la poursuite de l'amélioration de sa dynamique opérationnelle. Dans le même temps, la phase d'investissements intensifs engagée ces dernières années entre progressivement dans une nouvelle étape. Les investissements consolidés se sont établis à 1,7 milliard de dirhams au premier semestre 2026, en recul de 40 % par rapport au niveau particulièrement élevé enregistré un an plus tôt. Cette baisse est essentiellement liée à l'achèvement des travaux de construction des deux principaux projets stratégiques du groupe, Tizert et Boto, dont le développement avait mobilisé d'importantes ressources financières au cours des dernières années. Pour autant, Managem poursuit son programme de développement. Le groupe continue d'investir dans son projet de production de sulfate de cobalt, tout en faisant avancer la première phase du projet gazier de Tendrara, dont les premières productions sont attendues avant la fin de l'année. Selon le groupe, ces nouveaux projets doivent permettre d'élargir davantage son portefeuille d'activités et de consolider ses perspectives de croissance à moyen terme. Ils devraient également soutenir la génération de flux de trésorerie, contribuant à la poursuite du désendettement. Cette amélioration se reflète déjà dans la structure financière de Managem. À fin juin 2026, son endettement consolidé s'établissait à 9,9 milliards de dirhams, contre 12,6 milliards de dirhams à la clôture de l'exercice précédent, soit une diminution de 21 % depuis le début de l'année. Pour le groupe, cette évolution illustre les premiers effets de l'entrée en production de ses nouveaux actifs, qui renforcent sa capacité à générer des flux de trésorerie suffisants pour financer son expansion tout en réduisant progressivement son niveau d'endettement. Ainsi, après plusieurs années consacrées au développement de grands projets miniers, Managem amorce une nouvelle phase, davantage centrée sur la valorisation de ses investissements et l'amélioration de ses équilibres financiers. The post Managem franchit un seuil historique de 11,8 milliards de dirhams de chiffre d'affaires appeared first on Hespress Français - Actualités du Maroc .

items.title: AKSA Energy case: Ghana has evidence to trigger own accountability process – Osae-Kwapong
items.description: Democracy and Development Fellow at the Centre for Democratic Development (CDD-Ghana), John Osae-Kwapong, says Ghanaian law enforcement agencies already possess information that could form the basis for domestic investigations into the AKSA Energy-related bribery allegations. His comments follow disclosures that Ghanaian institutions, including the Office of the Special Prosecutor (OSP) and the Economic and Organised Crime Office (EOCO), collaborated with US authorities in investigations that contributed to the conviction of an individual over a bribery scheme linked to a power plant deal involving Ghana. According to Mr Osae-Kwapong, the collaboration demonstrates that Ghanaian law enforcement agencies have the capacity to investigate complex corruption cases and gather evidence capable of supporting criminal accountability. “For me, it says to me that these are agencies capable of conducting investigations and coming up with evidence needed to support holding persons accountable for allegedly having committed certain crimes,” he said. He, however, believes the collaboration with US authorities raises a further question about what Ghanaian institutions intend to do with the information they have gathered. Mr Osae-Kwapong said the disclosures by the OSP suggest that Ghana may already have preliminary information that could be used to initiate its own accountability processes. “If you look at the OSP statement, then it also says to me that these critical institutions are in possession of at least some information that can be the basis of triggering our own accountability processes within, you know, in Ghana,” he explained. He argued that Ghana should not simply rely on the outcome of the US proceedings but should use the information obtained through the collaboration to examine whether any Ghanaian individuals or institutions may have been involved in wrongdoing. “At least that’s my take on it, that if EOCO and other agencies, they help in terms of collaborating with the U.S. in pursuing this case against the said gentleman who has been convicted in the U.S., then it tells me that we do have some preliminary information that we can use as the first step towards also triggering our own accountability processes in Ghana,” he said. It follows the US conviction of former Tema Oil Refinery (TOR) Managing Director, Asante Kwaku Berko, in the high-profile international bribery case. The OSP said on Monday, August 10, that it assisted the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) with investigative and evidentiary material through Ghana’s established mutual legal assistance framework. According to the anti-corruption agency, the support provided by Ghana was specifically recognised by the United States Department of Justice (DoJ) as having played a significant role in the prosecution.

items.title: Troops rescue 16 kidnapped victims in Kogi
items.description: Troops have rescued 16 kidnapped persons after engaging suspected bandits in Dekina Local Government Area of Kogi. The victims comprised six males, six females and four children, according to an operational report made available to the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) on Monday. The report said the victims were abducted on Saturday, Aug. 9 along Ojuwo-Ajengo-Memarebo and Ojiwo-Itobe roads in Ofu Local Government Area of the state. It said the operation followed intelligence that the victims were sighted around Adumu community in Dekina. According to the report, the search-and-rescue operation involves troops of 21 Battalion and Nigerian Navy Ship (NNS) Lugard, the police, vigilantes and Hybrid Forces. “The security forces eventually made contact with the suspected kidnappers and engaged them, forcing the criminals to abandon their victims and flee. “However, one member of the Hybrid Forces was killed during the encounter, while one police personnel sustained injuries. “The rescued victims were subsequently handed over to the police in Ajaokuta for further action,” it said. The military said the operation highlights the continued collaboration among the military, police and local security groups in tackling kidnapping and rescuing victims in Kogi. (NAN) The post Troops rescue 16 kidnapped victims in Kogi appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: TUSAAG backs GAUA strike over unresolved pay disparities
items.description: The Technical Universities Senior Administrators Association of Ghana (TUSAAG) has declared its support for the ongoing strike action by the Ghana Association of University Administrators (GAUA), saying the two groups face similar concerns over pay disparities and conditions of service. In a statement dated August 9, TUSAAG said it “associates itself fully” with the industrial action and considers GAUA’s demands inseparable from its own concerns. The two associations jointly submitted a conditions of service proposal for negotiation, but according to TUSAAG, the proposal was rejected on grounds of transitional limitations on the part of the Fair Wages and Salaries Commission. An interim allowance was subsequently negotiated in place of the conditions of service agreement. TUSAAG said it and GAUA have since observed what it described as concerning pay disparities arising from the negotiations. “The unequal treatment and unresolved grievances that GAUA is contesting mirror the very concerns TUSAAG has raised through the same negotiations, and we recognize in GAUA’s decision to strike a struggle that is, in every practical sense, our own,” the statement said. The association said strike action was not taken lightly, arguing that it follows persistent concerns, stalled negotiations and the inability to safeguard members’ interests through dialogue alone. “Having sat at the same negotiating table and faced the same pay disparities, TUSAAG fully appreciates why GAUA has been left with no option but to withdraw its services,” it said. TUSAAG has consequently pledged to stand with GAUA, its leadership and members throughout the industrial action. It also said it regards GAUA’s demands as inseparable from its own and will not distance itself from the dispute. The association is calling on the relevant authorities and stakeholders to engage GAUA “in good faith, with urgency and sincerity” to resolve the pay disparities and other issues at the centre of the dispute. TUSAAG further said it would continue monitoring developments and remain ready to provide additional support towards what it described as a just resolution. The association also commended GAUA’s leadership for its resolve in defending the interests of its members and urged stakeholders in the tertiary education sector to support a swift and equitable resolution.

items.title: BoG and SEC roll out Ashanti NaVALI initiative to drive responsible virtual asset adoption
items.description: The Ashanti Regional phase of the National Virtual Asset Literacy Initiative (NaVALI) has been launched to protect financial stability in Ghana’s fast-growing digital finance sector. The initiative follows the enactment of the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act 2025 (Act 1154) and is aimed at ensuring that innovation in virtual assets progresses responsibly, with a strong emphasis on consumer protection and market integrity. The NaVALI is a collaborative initiative led by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) in partnership with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), academia and key industry stakeholders. It is anchored on two key objectives: strengthening institutional capacity in virtual assets and enabling technologies such as blockchain to ensure effective regulation and supervision, and driving nationwide awareness of the risks and implications of virtual assets to prevent uninformed and risky adoption as the sector evolves. The launch, held at University of Skills Training and Entrepreneurial Development (USTED) under the theme: “Understand before you undertake,” was attended by regulators, market players, consumer advocates, and members of the media. On the sidelines of the event, the Head of the Fintech and Innovation Department at the Bank of Ghana (BoG), Elhanan Owureku Asare, said regulators are establishing the necessary structures, systems, and processes to ensure the timely and orderly operationalisation of the new Act. He explained that NaVALI is designed to place education and awareness at the centre of the country’s digital finance regulatory framework. The goal, he noted, is to equip consumers, industry players, and public institutions with the knowledge needed to make informed decisions and avoid risky or uninformed participation in the virtual asset space. Owureku Asare stressed that a well-informed ecosystem is critical to safeguarding consumer protection, market integrity, and financial stability. “Effective regulation and enforcement cannot be achieved by regulators alone without a clear understanding of how virtual assets work and the risks they carry,” he said. He added that the initiative reflected a proactive and collaborative approach to ensuring that innovation in virtual assets progressed responsibly in the country. “NaVALI is a collaborative initiative being implemented by the Bank of Ghana (BoG) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) to intensify awareness around crypto and digital asset operations. Given that this is the new financial system in the modern world, we cannot do away with it. This strategic plan is therefore necessary to prevent operators from taking advantage of and defrauding Ghanaians,” Owureku Asare stated. Investing in Crypto The Deputy Director-General for Finance at the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), Mensah Thompson, cautioned Ghanaians interested in crypto and digital financial asset operations to be vigilant when investing. According to him, investors must verify the legitimacy of service providers before committing any funds. “Individuals interested in investing in crypto or digital assets must be vigilant. You must ensure that any Virtual Asset Service Provider you deal with is licensed by the appropriate regulatory authorities,” he said. He noted that licensing is key to protecting consumers from fraud and ensuring market integrity in the growing digital asset space. “We don’t want a situation where unlicensed operators take advantage of Ghanaians. That is why it is important for the public to check and confirm that any platform they use has approval from the Bank of Ghana or the SEC,” he added. Mr. Thompson stressed that regulation and public education must go hand in hand to build a safe and well-informed digital finance ecosystem. He also stressed that the Virtual Asset Service Providers Act represents a defining milestone that will reshape the country’s financial ecosystem, spanning banking, capital markets, and emerging digital finance activities. He said the legislation signalled a fundamental shift in how financial services would be delivered and regulated, with virtual assets and blockchain technology increasingly influencing traditional systems. Mr. Thompson expressed the commitment of the SEC to forge close collaboration with the BoG to support industry players and market operators as they adjusted to the new regulatory landscape. He said that the launch of the National Virtual Asset Literacy Initiative was critical to carrying the public along in this transition, stressing that education was indispensable to responsible innovation. “This initiative marks a significant step in our national journey to deepen understanding of virtual assets and their role within the broader financial system,” he said. Prospects for financial inclusion The Deputy Director-General explained that while virtual assets and new financial rails offered strong prospects for financial inclusion, efficiency and economic growth, they also carried risks to investor protection, market integrity and financial stability. For that reason, he said a comprehensive and well-coordinated national approach was required to balance innovation with effective safeguards. Prof. Joseph Antwi Baafi, Lead Knowledge Partner for NaVALI and Head of the Department of Economics at USTED, said the awareness drive will be decentralized to ensure that Ghanaians across the country are reached, regardless of location. “We will be carrying out this exercise in our various schools, marketplaces, churches, and other gathering places,” he said. “The idea is to take the conversation directly to the people, because digital finance is no longer limited to offices and banks,” he noted. Prof. Antwi Baafi added that “we cannot ignore digital assets. They are part of the new financial world. Our job is to make sure Ghanaians are not left behind, and that they are protected as they engage”. He also urged citizens to actively participate in the awareness programs, stressing that knowledge is the first line of defense against fraud. “This, I believe, will help them to understand digital money, virtual assets, the opportunities available, the risks involved, and the safety practices they need to adopt,” he explained. He said NaVALI’s role is to bridge that knowledge gap so people can make informed decisions and participate safely in the evolving financial system. Prof. Baafi, who co-authored the National Virtual Assets Education Manual, said the manual will be used as the primary resource for trainers and facilitators during the outreach. Dean of the School of Graduate Studies at USTEC, Prof. Humphrey Danso, added that the National Virtual Assets Education Manual, introduced under NaVALI, would serve as a structured tool for public education, policy engagement, and stakeholder dialogue. He cautioned against the damage caused by fraudulent investment schemes, adding that education, not fear, remains the best defense. “Many of us still recall the damage done by fraudulent investment schemes that impacted thousands of Ghanaian households. Today’s fraudster does not necessarily knock on your front door. They enter your mobile phone, appear on your social media timeline, create convincing websites, and impersonate respected institutions. They lure you with promises of huge returns, exploit trust, manipulate fear, and prey on your hope,” he observed. “The greatest weapon against such deception is not fear. It is education,” he concluded

items.title: Colombia earthquake death toll jumps to 111; president declares emergency
items.description: Colombia on Monday declared a state of emergency following a powerful earthquake that caused at least 111 deaths and flattened dozens of buildings, trapping more victims underneath. The 7.4-magnitude quake struck western Colombia at 7:34 am (1234 GMT) and triggered a frantic search for survivors in several cities. “The national government is maintaining all its capacities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid to every area that needs it,” President Abelardo de la Espriella stated from Bogota. The leader appointed just three days ago reported 111 deaths, 87 people injured and over 1,000 buildings were damaged. The quake’s epicenter was in Colombia’s coastal Choco region at a depth of 100 kilometers (60 miles). Authorities in the impoverished area reported 12 deaths. The nearby city of Pereira was one of the worst-hit areas, with local authorities earlier announcing that at least 40 people had died in the Risaralda region of which it is the provincial capital. The quake crumpled a tower of a beloved cathedral in the city of Manizales, an AFP journalist observed. “A great many buildings” in the city sustained damage, said administrative worker Jaime Zuluaga, 50. “Traffic is paralyzed and people don’t want to go back to their homes for fear of an aftershock.” – ‘Missing people’ – At least 20 buildings crumbled in Colombia’s third-largest city, Cali, trapping people beneath the debris, Mayor Alejandro Eder said. Choco’s governor warned of serious damage in the provincial capital Quibdo, where videos showed more buildings reduced to rubble. “We are all devastated,” Quibdo community leader Luis Gregorio Moreno told AFP. “At this moment there are reported deaths, dozens of wounded, but what there are most of are missing people,” he said. Ecuador, Panama and Venezuela also felt the early-morning quake, which prompted building evacuations in the Colombian capital, Bogota. Still wearing their pajamas, crowds of people rushed out into the street upon feeling the tremor, AFP reporters saw. “The quake was very, very strong,” said content creator Valeria Polo, 29, in the capital, where only minimal damage was recorded. Six small airports in western Colombia suspended operations, the civil aeronautics agency said, and the soccer governing body postponed upcoming football matches. Washington is “closely monitoring the large earthquake that struck Colombia and stands ready to support the people of Colombia,” US Secretary of State Marco Rubio wrote on X. European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU was “ready to provide more support” to the South American country. “We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations,” she wrote on social media. Israel, Mexico, Ecuador and France also offered assistance. Latin America is already reeling from two disastrous quakes that struck Venezuela in June, killing more than 6,000 people and causing widespread destruction. items.title: Russia blocks only anti-war party from elections
items.description: Russia’s Supreme Court on Monday barred the country’s only anti-war party, Yabloko, from contesting September’s parliamentary elections. The court thereby upheld a suit brought by a pro-Kremlin nationalist party, stripping voters opposed to the four-and-a-half-year war in Ukraine of their last option on the ballot. “The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted,” judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said. About a hundred supporters, mostly young people, gathered outside the courthouse, chanting “Shame! Shame!” after the ruling was delivered. Addressing them after the hearing, Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov said the party would appeal the decision. “We have a long way ahead and we have a big and important task: to stop deaths and bring the peace back,” he said. “Everything we do should be dedicated to that,” Rybakov added. With most of President Vladimir Putin’s opponents jailed, exiled or dead, Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia. The party has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya, the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny. Both are listed as “extremists” in Russia. A poll conducted earlier this year showed Yabloko (“apple” in Russian) at just three percent support — short of the five-percent threshold needed to enter Russia’s lower house. With the Kremlin tightening its control over elections, Yabloko has failed to win seats in the State Duma since 2003. Since then, every parliamentary vote has been won by the ruling United Russia party, which backs Putin. Efforts to end the Ukraine war through diplomacy have so far failed, with Putin pushing hardline territorial demands to end the fighting and ruling out talks with Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky. Independent polls show most Russians favour peace negotiations with Kyiv. AFP The post Russia blocks only anti-war party from elections appeared first on Vanguard News .
